Remember to check for any available planning data and applicable information from previous sprints or releases to facilitate the current release planning; this may include, but is not limited to:

  • Results of previous sprints and releases
  • Stakeholder feedback on the product, market situation or deadline(s)
  • Action plans and SMART goals from previous release and retrospective
  • Any items or defects to consider as lessons learned
  • Historic or estimated velocity, adjusting for any changes in the Development Team
  • Organizational and personal calendars to determine availability
  • Input from other teams and subject matter experts to identify dependencies

Remember that the:

  • Time needed for release planning may vary depending on the size of the project team, number of stakeholders, level of agreement on objectives and experience level of the teams and facilitator
  • Meeting is a high-level plan for future sprints reflecting expectations and forecast of product elements to be delivered, but not a commitment to deliver them
  • Identified risks and dependencies, if any, should be documented in the Product Backlog as appropriate

Schedule time with the appropriate stakeholders to conduct the release planning meeting. The initial release planning meeting(s) typically last no longer than one day or two half-days, if the stakeholders are unable to allocate an entire day.

During the meeting, review and understand:

  1. Original vision for the scope of work to guide planning
  2. Results from previous sprints and releases to understand velocity (pace of prior delivery) and how that may translate into expectations for the upcoming release(s)
  3. Any new information that may impact the plan
  4. Release strategy covering how the finished product(s) will be delivered to stakeholders and final users (e.g. continuous, phased of flexible)
  5. Time constraints on releasing completed Backlog Items either into the production system environment or to stakeholders and users of the output (for non-technical delivery)

It is important to consider the release strategy since it will impact the overall release planning, release strategy options include:

  • Continuous delivery (feature-driven)
  • Phased delivery (date-driven)
  • Flexible delivery (hybrid)

The approach selected above will dictate the form of the Release Plan. For a continuous, or feature-driven, approach divide the sum of all feature estimates by expected velocity to determine the number of sprints needed to deliver the requested functionality. Alternatively, for a phased, or date-drive, approach multiply the number of sprints by the expected velocity to determine the amount of work that can be delivered within the given timeline.

Next, agree on objectives to be achieved during the upcoming releases with more focus placed on the nearest release. Then, calculate the number of sprints required to deliver the entire Product Backlog based on any known velocity and key milestones, such as the expected release date for the product or upcoming market window. If the velocity is unknown, in the case of new or immature teams, be sure adequate discussions take place to agree upon the estimated velocity.

Select estimated Backlog Items to be included in each release, use agreed upon objectives and the ordered Product Backlog to guide this process. Again, maintain focus on the upcoming release, while information for later releases can be kept at a high level. Plan in a collaborative fashion where all participants can commonly understand how selected Backlog Items will enable the achievement of release objectives.

If it is determined that it will not be possible to complete all desired Backlog Items for a release, which is common, then decide to:

  • Reduce ambition for the release(s) through employing the Minimum Viable Product principle by matching the capacity of the Development Team to the Backlog Items assigned to the release (this is left up to the discretion of the Product Owner in discussion with the stakeholders and Development Team)
  • Simplify or remove some of the requirements, features, and so forth contained in the Product Backlog
  • Increase delivery capacity by adding resources to the Development Team, assigning Backlog Items to other existing Scrum teams or creating new Scrum teams (note: each of these will take time and will initially have the reverse effect)
  • Identify ways in which to increase velocity (note: as these are experiments, the actions will not guarantee results)

To facilitate the matching of delivery capacity with release objectives it may also be necessary to:

  • Identify risks
  • Identify dependencies
  • Engage in high-level planning to deal with identified risks and dependencies

As a Product Owner, be sure to:

  1. Present and explain the product vision, strategy and goals
  2. Be aware of, and share, key dates and milestones
  3. Select Backlog Items of the highest value, given the release scope constraints

As a Development Team member, be sure to:

  1. Ask questions to better understand Backlog Items, scope and requirements
  2. Estimate initial capacity and velocity per sprint
  3. Re-estimate Backlog Items as needed
  4. Document work selected for the release in a Burndown Chart as desired or requested

As a Scrum Master, be sure to:

  1. Facilitate the entire process by mediating the selection of approaches for each part of the release planning
  2. Confirm the planning is realistic and that the Development Team does not commit to a larger scope than they are comfortable with or have realistic chances of meeting 
  3. Elicit consensus and agreement from the team to proceed
